reason: Quotes state Kaia Health uses AWS KMS to encrypt its data to help comply with regulations in various countries and that DiGA certification requires control of its data; context calls it a German healthcare startup offering digital health applications.
Document history row 'Dual-stack support | AWS KMS supports dual-stack. | June 18, 2025' matches claim and date.
The row limits KEY_AGREEMENT to NIST-recommended ECC keys and SM2 keys in China Regions only; the claim and scope drop both conditions (date and DeriveSharedSecret are supported).
The row only says KMS supports the new KeySpec ECC_NIST_EDWARDS25519 on November 7, 2025; the parenthetical 'EdDSA signatures' is not stated in the quote or context.
Row states support for External key stores that protect AWS resources with keys outside of AWS, dated November 29, 2022.

Quotes support the FIPS 140-2 Level 2 since 2017 statement and today's FIPS 140-3 Level 3 protection, but neither quote nor context shows the 2023-05-24 date, an 'upgrade' announcement, or the 'outside the China Regions' scope (the FAQ says all Regions where KMS is offered).
Row dated June 5, 2023 adds importing key material for all types of KMS keys except custom key stores; asymmetric and HMAC keys are KMS key types, so the 'so' clause follows.
Rows of June 5, 2025 (on-demand rotation of symmetric keys with imported material, EXTERNAL origin) and November 26, 2025 (multi-Region keys with imported material) match both dates and parts.
Row dated July 8, 2022 states the KMS keys resource quota was increased to 100,000 KMS keys in each account and Region.

What's New post of Apr 27, 2026 states visibility into the last cryptographic operation (timestamp, operation type, CloudTrail event ID), no manual log queries, and the new kms:TrailingDaysWithoutKeyUsage condition key.
Row dated June 13, 2025 adds ML-DSA post-quantum cryptographic signatures.
Row dated July 8, 2024 increased the default cryptographic operations request rate for symmetric, RSA, and ECC and SM2 KMS keys.

Row supports custom rotation periods, on-demand rotation and 'visibility into your key material rotations' on April 12, 2024, but not the narrower 'list of completed rotations' wording or the 'customer managed symmetric encryption keys' scope.
The quote supports the old $1/month per rotation and the cap at the second rotation, but neither quote nor context shows the 2024-04-12 date value.
Row dated March 6, 2026 adds grants for service principals via GranteeServicePrincipal and RetiringServicePrincipal in CreateGrant and the SourceArn grant constraint.
Quotes define server-side encryption at the destination by the receiving service and client-side encryption as local encryption before the service receives it, with the service playing no role.
Quote states single-tenant HSM instances owned and managed by you and that the CloudHSM key store provides low TPS with availability, durability and performance dependent on your cluster.
Quote: key material never leaves your HSMs unencrypted and cryptographic operations are performed in the HSMs in the cluster.

FAQ answer says API requests are handled the same way, authentication and authorization operate independently of key location, activity is logged to CloudTrail the same way, and cryptographic operations happen in the custom key store.
Quote: create an active CloudHSM cluster; the cluster must have at least two active HSMs in different Availability Zones.
Quotes state CloudTrail records all calls to KMS by users, roles and services, and that by default all KMS actions are logged but can be excluded from a trail.
Quotes under kms:CallerAccount state it allows or denies access to all identities in an account, combined with a Principal element specifying all AWS identities.
Quote states kms:EncryptionContext:context-key can require a particular encryption context when controlling access to a symmetric encryption KMS key.
Claim restates the quote verbatim: kms:ViaService limits use of a KMS key to requests from specified AWS services.
KMS best-practice guide quote: S3 bucket keys can reduce costs by up to 99% and are a recommended alternative to disabling encryption; context ties it to high request volumes from S3.
Quote says SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT is the default value of KeySpec in CreateKey; context says the condition covers requests with no KeySpec parameter.
Quote: cross-account access requires permission in the key policy and in an IAM policy in the external user's account.
Quotes and context list cryptographic operations, CreateGrant, DescribeKey etc. as the only effective cross-account operations and say other permissions such as ScheduleKeyDeletion have no effect.
Quote: for cross-account requests KMS throttles the account that makes the requests, not the key owner account.
RDS quote: to copy an encrypted snapshot across Regions you must specify the KMS key in the destination Region because KMS keys are Region-specific.
The FAQ answer sits under 'custom key store backed by CloudHSM'; the claim says 'each custom key store requires a CloudHSM cluster' without that scope, which would wrongly cover external key stores.
Quotes: only customer managed keys can be stored in a CloudHSM-backed custom key store; AWS managed keys are always generated and stored in the default key store.
Quote lists setting up a cluster, adding HSMs, managing HSM users, potentially restoring from backup, and calls these security sensitive tasks.
Quote: consider a custom key store only when regulations explicitly mandate single-tenant or outside-AWS HSM protection and the risk outweighs added cost, complexity and reduced performance.
Quote: two custom key store types, CloudHSM key stores backed by a customer-owned cluster and external key stores backed by an HSM or key manager outside the AWS Cloud.
Quotes: customer managed keys are created, owned and managed by you, with full control over policies, grants, enable/disable, rotation, tags, aliases and deletion scheduling.
Quote: if exceeding the GenerateDataKey quota, consider data key caching of the AWS Encryption SDK; reusing data keys might reduce request frequency.
Quotes under the critical default statement: gives the owning account full access and allows IAM policies to allow access in addition to the key policy.
Quote matches the claim: reduces risk of the key becoming unmanageable by giving access to account administrators including the root user, which cannot be deleted.

Quote supports destructive, irreversible deletion and unrecoverable data, but the very next sentence names exceptions (multi-Region replica keys, asymmetric and HMAC keys with imported key material) that the claim drops.
